name: Frontend developer
summary: Frontend developer interviews usually test JavaScript, HTML and CSS fundamentals, then a framework such as React, often through a live exercise building or fixing a small component. Candidates commonly report questions on how the browser works, performance and accessibility, and for experienced roles, how they'd structure a larger app.
rounds: Online test or take-home: JavaScript questions or a small interface to build (often)
Live coding: build or debug a component, sometimes in plain JavaScript
Frontend fundamentals and framework discussion: the browser, CSS, state and performance
Frontend system design for experienced roles: structuring a larger app or feature
looks_for: Solid JavaScript: scope, closures, the event loop, promises and async/await
Semantic HTML and CSS layout you can explain, not just copy
Thinking in components: state, props and where data should live
Care for users: accessibility, loading states, errors and slow networks
Knowing what makes a page slow and how to measure it
Working well with designers and backend developers

questions.text: Tell me about a time a design you were given was hard to build as drawn. What did you do?
covers: What made it hard: a layout, an animation, small screens, an accessibility problem
How you raised it with the designer and what you proposed
What shipped, and whether users or the team noticed a difference

questions.text: Describe a UI bug that only some users saw. How did you find and fix it?
covers: How it was reported and why it didn't show on your machine
How you reproduced it: browser, device, network speed, user data
The cause, the fix and how you stopped it recurring

questions.text: Tell me about a time you made a page or app noticeably faster.
covers: How you measured it before and after
What was slow: large bundles, heavy images, too many re-renders, slow API calls
The result in numbers, such as load time or a performance score

questions.text: Tell me about a time you and a backend developer had to agree on what an API should return.
covers: What the screen needed and what the API offered at first
How you agreed the shape of the data, errors and loading behaviour
What you'd settle earlier next time

questions.text: Explain closures in JavaScript with an example of where you've used one.
covers: A function keeping access to variables from the place it was created
A practical use: event handlers, private state, a debounce function
A common pitfall, such as stale values inside a React effect or a loop

questions.text: How does the JavaScript event loop work, and why doesn't a slow network call freeze the page?
covers: One main thread, a call stack, and queues of waiting callbacks
Promise callbacks (microtasks) running before timers and other tasks
Why heavy computation does freeze the page, and what you'd do about it

questions.text: What's the difference between let, const and var, and between == and ===?
covers: Block scope versus function scope, and hoisting
const stops reassignment but doesn't make an object unchangeable
== converts types before comparing and === doesn't, and why most teams prefer ===

questions.text: How would you centre an element, and build a layout that works on both mobile and desktop?
covers: Flexbox or grid, and when you'd pick each
Mobile-first styles with media queries and relative units
Testing on real devices, not only by resizing the browser window

questions.text: In React, when does a component re-render, and how would you stop unnecessary re-renders?
covers: State or props changing, or a parent re-rendering
Measuring with the profiler before optimising
Memoisation, stable callbacks and splitting state, and the cost of overusing them

questions.text: Where would you keep state in a mid-sized app: inside components, in context, in a store, or in a server cache? How do you decide?
covers: Keeping state as close as possible to where it's used
Treating server data differently from UI state, and tools that cache server data
When a shared store is worth its extra complexity

questions.text: What would you check to make a form usable for someone with a screen reader or only a keyboard?
covers: Labels tied to inputs, semantic elements and a sensible tab order
Error messages that are announced and not shown only in red
Testing with a keyboard and a screen reader yourself

questions.text: A page takes several seconds to load on a mid-range phone. How would you find out why and speed it up?
covers: Measuring with browser dev tools and a performance audit on a throttled connection
Common causes: large JavaScript bundles, unoptimised images, render-blocking scripts, slow APIs
Fixes such as code splitting, lazy loading, compression and caching, in order of impact

questions.text: Talk me through how you'd build a search box that shows suggestions as the user types.
covers: Debouncing input, and cancelling or ignoring out-of-date responses
Loading, empty and error states, and moving through suggestions with the keyboard
Caching recent results and keeping it accessible

questions.text: How does the browser turn HTML, CSS and JavaScript into pixels, and what makes that slow?
covers: Building the DOM and CSSOM, then style, layout, paint and compositing
What forces extra layout work, such as reading sizes straight after changing styles
Why scripts can block rendering, and how defer or async helps

questions.text: What are the main security risks in frontend code, and how do you guard against them?
covers: Cross-site scripting from inserting untrusted HTML, and how frameworks escape output
Keeping secrets out of frontend code and being careful where tokens are stored
CSRF and CORS in plain words, and what the backend must still check

questions.text: Why frontend? What do you enjoy about building interfaces?
covers: Something you built that people used, and what you learned from watching them
The part you enjoy most: visual craft, performance, accessibility, design systems
What you want to get better at next

questions.text: Which website or app has an interface you admire, and what would you improve about ours?
covers: A specific example and what makes it work for its users
One concrete improvement to the company's product, with the reason
How you'd check the change helped

tips: Practise building a small component from scratch without a framework; some live rounds use plain JavaScript.
Mention the states as you build: loading, empty, error and success. Interviewers notice when you handle them unprompted.
Keep one project with a live link ready, and be able to explain its folder structure and where its state lives.
When asked about performance, say how you'd measure first; numbers from dev tools beat guesses.
Revise accessibility basics; many candidates skip them, so a good answer stands out.
